title: Putting it together: a full passage set
blurb: Work a whole HESI passage set at exam pace: one careful read, paragraph gists, then main idea, detail and inference items answered from the right place.
question: A 400-word HESI A2 passage about night-shift naps is followed by six questions: a main idea, a detail, a word in context, two inferences and the author's purpose. You have about six and a half minutes. How do you read it, in what order do you think, and how do you keep the main idea and inference answers from falling into the classic traps?

teach.body: Formally, a passage set is one reading passage followed by several questions, each testing a different reading skill. HESI A2 passages run about 250-500 words on health, science or general-interest topics; prep sources report about 5-8 questions per passage. In plain English: you read once, carefully, and that one read pays off across many questions. The two anchors of most sets are the main idea (what the whole passage says) and the inference (what it implies).

teach.h: A HESI Reading set by the numbers

teach.body:
(1) For nurses, paramedics and other night-shift workers, the hours between 3 and 5 a.m. are often the hardest. The body's internal clock pushes alertness to its lowest point then, however much coffee is on the counter.

(2) Some hospitals now allow short, planned naps during night shifts. A nap of about 20 to 30 minutes can sharpen alertness without leaving the sleeper groggy. Longer naps carry a cost: waking from deep sleep can cause sleep inertia, a foggy feeling that may last up to half an hour.

(3) Nap programs are not simple to run. Units need a quiet room, a way to cover patients while a nurse rests, and a culture in which resting is not seen as laziness. Hospitals that have solved these problems report that staff feel safer driving home in the morning.

head: Skill
Stem on the nap passage
Where to look
rows: How long is the nap advised?
What is implied about long naps?
teach.caption: Detail and word items send you back to one place; main idea items need the whole passage.

teach.h: A plan for the whole set
items: Read the passage once at a steady pace (about two minutes for 400 words).
After each paragraph, say its gist to yourself in 3-5 words.
Detail and word items: go back to the named paragraph and reread only the lines you need.
Main idea items: pick the option that covers every gist, not just the one you reread last.
Inference items: pick the option the clues most strongly support, then check that no paragraph contradicts it.
Keep moving: if one item stalls you past about 90 seconds, choose the best remaining option and go on.

teach.h: From gists to the main idea

steps.label: Gist 2
steps.sub: Short naps help; long naps fog

steps.label: Main idea
steps.sub: Planned short naps help, but take work

teach.h: The two anchors: main idea and inference
teach.body: A main idea answer must cover every paragraph: 'Short naps can sharpen alertness' is too narrow, and 'Sleep matters for health' is too broad. A best title names the topic and that main idea. An inference answer is not written in the passage but is the option the clues most strongly support: the passage implies that a nurse woken from a long nap may be less alert for a while, because longer naps reach deep sleep and sleep inertia can last up to half an hour.

teach.h: Main idea vs inference in one set

teach.text: Two passage-set traps: (1) a 'main idea' that repeats the paragraph you just reread for a detail item, which is too narrow; (2) an 'inference' that copies a sentence you just reread, which is stated, not implied. What is fresh in your mind is not automatically the answer.

teach.h: Scenario: Priya works the nap set
teach.body: Priya Natarajan, applying to a practical nursing program, reads the nap passage once and notes three gists. She answers the detail item from paragraph 2 (20 to 30 minutes) and the word item ('culture' means shared attitudes, not something grown in a lab). For the main idea, she rejects 'Long naps can cause sleep inertia' as too narrow. For 'What can be inferred about nap programs?', she rejects 'Most hospitals now offer them' (overreach) and picks 'They need planning beyond setting aside time to sleep.' She finishes in about six minutes.

items: Read the passage once, carefully, and note a 3-5 word gist for each paragraph.
Detail and word items: return to the named paragraph; main idea items: use every gist.
Main idea and best title: not too narrow, not too broad, covering the whole passage.
Inference: most strongly supported by the clues, not stated, not merely possible.
Pace: about 65 seconds per item including reading; do not reread the whole passage for each item.

summary: You can now work a full HESI passage set at exam pace: one careful read with paragraph gists, quick returns to the right paragraph for details, and main idea and inference answers that cover the whole passage or rest on its clues. You can also spot the too-narrow main idea and the stated-not-implied inference that sets use as traps.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) In many rural counties, paramedics now do more than answer 911 calls. In community paramedic programs, they visit patients at home after a hospital stay, checking blood pressure, reviewing medicines and making sure follow-up appointments are scheduled.

(2) The visits focus on patients who are most likely to return to the hospital, such as older adults with heart failure. In one county program, the share of these patients readmitted within 30 days fell from about one in four to about one in eight over two years.

(3) Funding remains the hardest problem. Insurers usually pay for an ambulance ride to the hospital but not for a paramedic's visit that keeps a patient at home.

What is the main idea of the passage about community paramedics?
options: Paramedics in rural counties answer more 911 calls than before.
Home visits by paramedics can cut hospital returns but are hard to fund.
Older adults with heart failure often return to the hospital.
Insurers should pay paramedics for every visit made to a home.
A.why: Paragraph 1 describes the home visits, paragraph 2 shows they cut readmissions, and paragraph 3 names funding as the hardest problem. The key covers all three gists.

whyNot.0: Distortion: paragraph 1 says paramedics now do more than answer 911 calls, not that they answer more of them.
whyNot.2: Too narrow: one detail from paragraph 2 about who the visits focus on.
whyNot.3: A recommendation the author does not make; paragraph 3 describes the funding gap without proposing a fix.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) In many rural counties, paramedics now do more than answer 911 calls. In community paramedic programs, they visit patients at home after a hospital stay, checking blood pressure, reviewing medicines and making sure follow-up appointments are scheduled.

(2) The visits focus on patients who are most likely to return to the hospital, such as older adults with heart failure. In one county program, the share of these patients readmitted within 30 days fell from about one in four to about one in eight over two years.

(3) Funding remains the hardest problem. Insurers usually pay for an ambulance ride to the hospital but not for a paramedic's visit that keeps a patient at home.

What can be inferred from paragraph 3 of the passage about community paramedics?
options: Some programs may struggle to continue without new funding.
Insurers have stopped paying for ambulance rides to hospitals.
Paramedic home visits cost more than ambulance rides do.
Patients prefer home visits to trips back to the hospital.
A.why: Funding is called the hardest problem, and insurers usually do not pay for the visits. It follows that some programs may have trouble continuing unless they find other money.

whyNot.1: Contradicts paragraph 3, which says insurers usually do pay for ambulance rides.
whyNot.2: Unsupported: the passage gives no costs for either service.
whyNot.3: Possible but unsupported: patients' preferences are not mentioned.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) In many rural counties, paramedics now do more than answer 911 calls. In community paramedic programs, they visit patients at home after a hospital stay, checking blood pressure, reviewing medicines and making sure follow-up appointments are scheduled.

(2) The visits focus on patients who are most likely to return to the hospital, such as older adults with heart failure. In one county program, the share of these patients readmitted within 30 days fell from about one in four to about one in eight over two years.

(3) Funding remains the hardest problem. Insurers usually pay for an ambulance ride to the hospital but not for a paramedic's visit that keeps a patient at home.

Which title best fits the passage about community paramedics?
options: The History of the 911 Emergency System
Heart Failure in Older Adults
Why Insurers Pay for Ambulance Rides
Paramedics Who Keep Patients Home
A.why: The passage is about paramedics visiting patients at home to keep them from returning to the hospital. The title names that topic and its point.

whyNot.0: Too broad and off-topic: 911 calls are mentioned once, and the passage gives no history.
whyNot.1: Too narrow: heart failure patients are one example in paragraph 2.
whyNot.2: Too narrow and off-center: insurance comes up in paragraph 3, and the passage does not explain why insurers pay for rides.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Every Tuesday, Gloria Mendez, a retired schoolteacher, sets up a folding table in the waiting room of the Eastside children's clinic. On it she spreads picture books in English and Spanish, and she reads aloud to any child who wanders over.

(2) At first, most parents kept their children on their laps and their eyes on their phones. By the third month, several families were arriving early on Tuesdays, and the front desk began booking routine checkups on that day when parents asked.

(3) Gloria lets each child take one book home. 'A book on the shelf at home,' she says, 'is an invitation that doesn't expire.'

What can be inferred about the families who began arriving early on Tuesdays?
options: They wanted their children to have time at Gloria's table.
They had been told by the clinic to come in on Tuesdays.
They could not afford to buy books for their children.
They preferred Gloria to the clinic's doctors and nurses.
B.why: Families arrived early on the day Gloria reads, and parents asked for checkups on that day. The clues point to wanting time at her table before the visit.

whyNot.1: Reversal: the front desk booked Tuesdays because parents asked, not the other way around.
whyNot.2: Unsupported: the passage says nothing about what families can afford.
whyNot.3: Overreach: enjoying the reading table does not show a preference over the clinic's staff.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Every Tuesday, Gloria Mendez, a retired schoolteacher, sets up a folding table in the waiting room of the Eastside children's clinic. On it she spreads picture books in English and Spanish, and she reads aloud to any child who wanders over.

(2) At first, most parents kept their children on their laps and their eyes on their phones. By the third month, several families were arriving early on Tuesdays, and the front desk began booking routine checkups on that day when parents asked.

(3) Gloria lets each child take one book home. 'A book on the shelf at home,' she says, 'is an invitation that doesn't expire.'

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage about Gloria Mendez?
options: Gloria Mendez taught school for many years before she retired.
Parents at the clinic spent much of their waiting time on phones.
Gloria's reading table drew families in and sent books home.
Clinics should replace their waiting room screens with books.
B.why: Paragraph 1 sets up the reading table, paragraph 2 shows families coming to it, and paragraph 3 shows books going home. The key covers all three.

whyNot.0: Too narrow, and it adds 'many years': the passage only calls her a retired schoolteacher.
whyNot.1: Too narrow: a detail about the early months in paragraph 2.
whyNot.3: A recommendation the passage does not make; it describes one volunteer's table.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Every Tuesday, Gloria Mendez, a retired schoolteacher, sets up a folding table in the waiting room of the Eastside children's clinic. On it she spreads picture books in English and Spanish, and she reads aloud to any child who wanders over.

(2) At first, most parents kept their children on their laps and their eyes on their phones. By the third month, several families were arriving early on Tuesdays, and the front desk began booking routine checkups on that day when parents asked.

(3) Gloria lets each child take one book home. 'A book on the shelf at home,' she says, 'is an invitation that doesn't expire.'

What does Gloria suggest by calling a book at home 'an invitation that doesn't expire'?
options: A book should be returned to the clinic by a set date.
A book will last longer than most of a child's toys.
A book invites the child back to the clinic each week.
A book keeps offering a child the chance to read again.
B.why: An invitation asks someone to join in; one that does not expire stays open. A book on the shelf keeps offering the child the chance to read, long after the clinic visit.

whyNot.0: Reversal: Gloria lets each child keep the book, and 'doesn't expire' means there is no deadline.
whyNot.1: Too literal: the phrase is about the book's ongoing invitation to read, not its durability compared with toys.
whyNot.2: Distortion: the invitation is to read at home, not to return to the clinic.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Hospitals are rarely quiet. Alarms, carts, overhead pages and conversations at the nurses' station can push noise on a unit well above the levels the World Health Organization recommends for patient rooms at night.

(2) Several hospitals have tried 'quiet hours,' usually from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Lights are dimmed, nonurgent tasks such as routine vital signs are grouped together, and staff lower their voices. Patients on these units report sleeping better, and some studies have found fewer requests for sleep medicine.

(3) Quiet hours ask something of everyone. Nurses must plan their work differently, and visitors may be asked to leave earlier. Still, for patients whose bodies are trying to heal, a full night of rest may be one of the simplest treatments a hospital can offer.

What is the main idea of the passage about hospital quiet hours?
options: Hospital noise often goes above the levels advised for patient rooms.
Quiet hours help patients rest, though they require effort from all.
Nurses should check vital signs less often during the night hours.
Hospitals have become noisier over time than they were in the past.
C.why: Paragraph 1 sets out the noise problem, paragraph 2 describes quiet hours and their benefits, and paragraph 3 notes the effort they take and their value. The key covers the whole passage.

whyNot.0: Too narrow: this is the problem described in paragraph 1, not the point of the passage.
whyNot.2: Distortion: routine tasks are grouped together at night, not done less often.
whyNot.3: Unsupported: the passage does not compare today's noise with the past.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Hospitals are rarely quiet. Alarms, carts, overhead pages and conversations at the nurses' station can push noise on a unit well above the levels the World Health Organization recommends for patient rooms at night.

(2) Several hospitals have tried 'quiet hours,' usually from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Lights are dimmed, nonurgent tasks such as routine vital signs are grouped together, and staff lower their voices. Patients on these units report sleeping better, and some studies have found fewer requests for sleep medicine.

(3) Quiet hours ask something of everyone. Nurses must plan their work differently, and visitors may be asked to leave earlier. Still, for patients whose bodies are trying to heal, a full night of rest may be one of the simplest treatments a hospital can offer.

What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about grouping routine tasks at night?
options: It means routine vital signs are skipped for most patients.
It was the main reason requests for sleep medicine fell.
It cuts the number of times a patient's sleep is broken.
It lets hospitals schedule fewer nurses on night shifts.
C.why: Grouping nonurgent tasks means staff enter the room fewer times during the night, which is why it belongs on a list of steps that help patients sleep.

whyNot.0: Overreach: grouping tasks means doing them together, not skipping them.
whyNot.1: Overreach: several changes happened together, so the passage cannot single out one as the main reason.
whyNot.3: Unsupported: paragraph 3 says nurses must plan their work differently, not that fewer nurses are needed.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Hospitals are rarely quiet. Alarms, carts, overhead pages and conversations at the nurses' station can push noise on a unit well above the levels the World Health Organization recommends for patient rooms at night.

(2) Several hospitals have tried 'quiet hours,' usually from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Lights are dimmed, nonurgent tasks such as routine vital signs are grouped together, and staff lower their voices. Patients on these units report sleeping better, and some studies have found fewer requests for sleep medicine.

(3) Quiet hours ask something of everyone. Nurses must plan their work differently, and visitors may be asked to leave earlier. Still, for patients whose bodies are trying to heal, a full night of rest may be one of the simplest treatments a hospital can offer.

Calling a full night of rest 'one of the simplest treatments a hospital can offer' suggests that the author:
options: thinks medicine matters less than sleep for healing
doubts that quiet hours work on busy hospital units
wants visiting hours ended on all hospital units
believes rest aids healing and is worth the effort
C.why: The word 'Still' turns from the costs to the value: despite the effort, rest is worth offering because it helps healing bodies.

whyNot.0: Overreach: calling rest a simple treatment does not rank it above medicine.
whyNot.1: Opposite: the author reports better sleep on quiet-hour units and argues the effort is worthwhile.
whyNot.2: Overstatement: visitors may be asked to leave earlier, not have visiting hours ended.

reteach.title: One trip through the store
reteach.question: You have a grocery list of six items. Is it faster to read the whole list once and walk the store, or to run in for one item, come out, and run in again for the next? How is that like a HESI passage set?

blocks.body: A shopper who reads the whole list first knows which aisles to visit and picks up everything in one smooth trip. A shopper who rereads the list and crosses the whole store for each item runs out of time. A passage set works the same way: one careful read with paragraph gists is your map of the aisles. Each question is then a short trip back to one paragraph, and the main idea question is the checkout, where you make sure your basket covers the whole list.

steps.label: Read the list once
steps.sub: One careful read of the passage

steps.label: Short trips
steps.sub: Back to one paragraph per item

blocks.text: Rereading the whole passage for every question burns the time you need for the last items in the set.

explain.body: As you read, sum up each paragraph in 3-5 words. The main idea is the one statement that covers every gist; an option that matches only one gist is too narrow.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Fresh fruits and vegetables often cost more per calorie than many packaged foods, and families on tight budgets tend to buy less produce as a result.

(2) Some farmers markets now match food assistance dollars spent on produce, so a family that spends $10 receives $20 worth of fruits and vegetables. Markets with these programs report more shoppers using food assistance and higher sales for local farmers.

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Packaged foods cost less per calorie than fresh produce does.
Matching programs help families afford produce and help farmers.
Farmers markets sell healthier food than grocery stores do.
Families on tight budgets buy too much packaged food each week.
test.why: Paragraph 1 sets up the cost problem and paragraph 2 describes matching programs that help both families and farmers. The key covers both gists.

whyNot.0: Too narrow: the background fact from paragraph 1.
whyNot.2: Unsupported: the passage does not compare farmers markets with grocery stores.
whyNot.3: Adds a judgment ('too much') the passage does not make.

explain.body: A best title names the topic and points to the main idea. Too broad fits a whole book; too narrow fits one paragraph; off-center grabs a vivid detail.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) In movies, a drowning person splashes, shouts and waves for help. In real life, drowning is usually quiet. A person struggling to keep the mouth above water cannot take in enough air to call out, and the arms press down on the water instead of waving.

(2) Lifeguards are trained to watch for a head tilted back at the water line and a body that stays upright without kicking. Parents at a pool can learn to watch for the same signs.

Which title best fits the passage?
options: Water Safety for the Whole Family
How Lifeguards Are Trained
The Quiet Signs of Drowning
Why Movies Get Swimming Wrong
test.why: Both paragraphs are about how drowning really looks (quiet, no waving, head back, upright body) and how to spot it. The title names that topic and point.

whyNot.0: Too broad: the passage covers one danger, not water safety in general.
whyNot.1: Too narrow: lifeguard training is one sentence in paragraph 2.
whyNot.3: Off-center: movies are the opening contrast, and the passage is about drowning, not swimming.

explain.body: Inference items in a set often point to one paragraph. Reread it, ask what the clues require, and choose the most strongly supported option, not one that is stated or merely possible.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The pharmacy on Grant Street began staying open until midnight in March.

(2) Within weeks, staff at the urgent care clinic next door, which closes at 11 p.m., noticed that patients they treated late in the evening no longer asked where they could fill a prescription that night.

What can be inferred from the passage?
options: Before March, late patients had trouble filling prescriptions that night.
The urgent care clinic began staying open until midnight in March.
The pharmacy stayed open later because the clinic asked it to.
Most of the pharmacy's customers are patients from the clinic.
test.why: Late patients used to ask where to fill a prescription that night and stopped once the pharmacy stayed open. That implies they had trouble finding an open pharmacy before.

whyNot.1: Contradicts paragraph 2: the clinic closes at 11 p.m.
whyNot.2: Unsupported: the passage gives no reason for the pharmacy's new hours.
whyNot.3: Overreach: the passage describes the clinic's late patients, not the pharmacy's customers as a whole.

explain.body: Sometimes no sentence states the main idea. Each paragraph adds a piece; the main idea is the statement that ties all the pieces together without adding a judgment the passage does not make.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Maya's grandfather keeps a pill organizer on the kitchen table, and every Sunday night Maya sorts his medicines into it.

(2) Her aunt calls each evening at 8 o'clock to ask whether the evening pills are gone.

(3) At the pharmacy, his refills are packed in bubble packs labeled by day and time, so a missed dose is easy to spot.

Which statement best expresses the implied main idea of the passage?
options: Maya's grandfather takes more medicines than he needs.
Several people help Maya's grandfather take his medicines.
Bubble packs are the best way to organize daily medicines.
Maya's aunt worries about him more than Maya does.
test.why: Maya sorts the pills, her aunt calls to check, and the pharmacy packs doses by time. Together the paragraphs show several people supporting his medicine routine.

whyNot.0: Adds a judgment the passage does not make; it describes his routine, not whether his medicines are needed.
whyNot.2: Overgeneralization: bubble packs are one support among several, and the passage does not rank methods.
whyNot.3: Unsupported comparison: both Maya and her aunt help; the passage does not compare their worry.
